ch13.title: The Mount of Transfiguration
ch13.b002: It was near sundown on Friday, August 12, when they reached the foot of Mount Hermon. Before Philip had even set down his load he was looking around: where they could draw water, whether there was enough dry wood for a fire, where thirteen men could find level ground to sleep. He was the steward of the apostolic company. However holy a mountain might be, people still had to eat supper. Cold spring water was welling up from a cleft in the rocks. Philip put his hand in it and nodded. There would be enough tonight.
ch13.b003: The place was close to the spot where, years before, a lad named Tiglath had waited while the Master went up the mountain alone. They stayed there two days. In a general way the Master knew beforehand what was to happen on the mountain, and he greatly wished that all his apostles might share it. That was why he lingered with them at the foot of the mountain, preparing them. But they could not reach the spiritual level that would have fitted them to face the full visitation of heavenly beings on earth. In the end he decided to take only the three who usually went with him when he withdrew to pray alone: Peter, James and John.
ch13.b004: Andrew nodded when he heard it. He was the one who had arranged it that way from the start, three men to stay close to the Master as his personal aides. So he had no reason to feel slighted, and in fact he did not. If anything he was glad that his brother would be going up the mountain with the Master. Peter was a man who drew strength from such things, and lately Peter needed strength. What worried Andrew was something else. Nine would be left behind. A camp with neither the Master nor Peter. He remembered the two weeks at Caesarea-Philippi, and how low the company had sunk with only Peter missing.
ch13.b005: Philip felt otherwise. Watching the three get ready, he could not keep from counting. What would they see? What was the Master going up there to receive? He wanted to see it. He always did. He was a man who had to see a thing with his own eyes to know it. And once again the place where the seeing happened was not to be his. Philip put a few loaves of dry bread, some dried figs and a skin of water into a sack and handed it to John. That much he could do: fill the stomachs of the men who were climbing the mountain.
ch13.b007: Early on the morning of Monday, August 15, the Master and the three apostles began to climb Hermon. It was six days since Peter’s confession under the mulberry trees.
ch13.b008: James Zebedee walked at the rear. On a climb he was sparing of words. It was not to save his breath. He was simply a man whose talkative days and silent days came by turns, and this was a silent one. Ahead of him went the Master’s back, then Peter, and just in front of him his brother John. Every so often John looked back over his shoulder. It was an old habit of his, making sure his brother was still there. Each time, James gave him a small nod.
ch13.b009: The path was steep. On the lower slopes the oaks stood here and there, but the higher they went the fewer the trees and the more bare rock showed through. Though it was August, the wind was cool. A little before noon they reached their destination, about halfway up the mountain. Over lunch the Master told them something of what he had gone through in the hills east of the Jordan just after his baptism, and something more of his earlier visit to this lonely mountain.
ch13.b010: James listened closely. He had known this man longer than almost anyone. With John he had known the Jesus who once worked in their father’s boatshop, a young craftsman building boats. And now that same man was telling of what he had gone through alone in the wilderness and on this very mountain. James thought about how much had lain hidden between the Jesus he knew and the Jesus who was speaking now. He could not know all of it. He only felt that what lay hidden there was not frightening, but quietly deep.
ch13.b011: About three o’clock the Master rose. He was going apart by himself, he said, to commune with the Father and his messengers. They were to stay here and pray, while they waited, that the Father’s will might be done in everything concerning the mission of the Son of Man. And he disappeared beyond the rocks.
ch13.b012: The three waited. The sun sank. One hour passed, then two. Peter was the first to grow restless. Again and again he got up and looked toward the rocks. John sat hugging his knees. James tried to pray, but some other thought kept rising at the edge of his mind. What if the Master did not come back? It was an absurd thought, and it would not go away.
ch13.b013: About six o’clock the Master returned. He looked at their faces and asked why they had been afraid. They knew very well that he must be about his Father’s business; why then did they doubt whenever he was not with them? And he told them that the Son of Man had now chosen to live out his whole life in their midst and as one of them. Be of good cheer, he said; he would not leave them until his work was finished.
ch13.b014: James set those words in his heart. Until his work was finished. What that end might be, he did not ask.
ch13.b015: Over their meager supper Peter asked how long they would stay on this mountain, away from their brothers. The Master answered: until they had seen the glory of the Son of Man and knew that everything he had told them was true. They sat around the glowing embers until darkness came, talking about the Lucifer rebellion. They had been walking since before dawn, and their eyelids grew heavy. John fell asleep first, then Peter. James watched the embers die down and was the last to close his eyes.
ch13.b017: When they had been asleep for about half an hour, there was a crackling sound close by. All three woke at once.
ch13.b018: At first James thought it was the fire spitting. But the embers had nearly gone out. He raised himself up. And he saw. A little way off stood the Master, and beside him were two beings. They had the form of men, but they were not men. They seemed clothed in garments woven of the light of the heavenly world. And the Master’s face and his whole form were shining with a heavenly light.
ch13.b019: James could not breathe. The light did not hurt his eyes. Rather, it would not let him close them. The three were talking together in a strange language. He could not understand a single word. But the tone was warm, like old friends. James was afraid of what he saw. Not because of the heavenly beings, but because of the Master, talking with them so intimately. The man who had once mended nets alongside him was speaking their language now. Who was he? Six days ago under the mulberry trees they had confessed him the Son of God. But James had not known that the confession would look like this.
ch13.b020: From a few things that were said, Peter guessed that the two were Moses and Elijah. He was wrong. They were Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek. The three apostles were able to witness the scene only because the Master had asked that it be so arranged.
ch13.b021: When the shining vision faded and they saw the Master standing alone, Peter, the first to collect his wits, found his voice. Master, he said, it was good to have been here; they rejoiced to see this glory, and they did not want to go back down to the inglorious world. If the Master was willing, let them stay, and they would put up three tents: one for him, one for Moses, one for Elijah. Peter said it because he was confused. At that moment nothing else came into his head.
ch13.b022: While Peter was still speaking, a silvery cloud drew near and overshadowed the four of them. James felt a cold mist touch his skin. He could see nothing before him. The three fell on their faces. Then they heard a voice, the same voice that was said to have spoken on the day of the Master’s baptism. It said that this was the beloved Son, and that they should give heed to him.
ch13.b023: James lay face down and smelled the earth. His forehead was pressed against cold stone. He did not weep. He made no sound. Only his whole body shook. All his life he had been a man who looked at everything from every side. When something happened he looked at it from this side and from that, and weighed it without hurrying. But now there was nothing to weigh. The voice came from one side only. And that was enough. Give heed to him. James received the words with his forehead to the ground. He had believed that he was already listening to this man. Tonight he learned how little he had heard.
ch13.b024: The cloud lifted. The Master was alone with the three again. He reached down and touched them. James felt the hand on his shoulder. It was warm. The hand that a moment before had been clothed in heavenly light was simply a man’s hand. Get up, the Master told them, and do not be afraid; they would see greater things than this. But they were truly afraid. A little before midnight they got ready to go down the mountain, three men silent and lost in thought.
ch13.b026: For about half the way down no one spoke. There were a great many stars. The stones underfoot glimmered faintly. Then the Master broke the silence. They were to tell no one, not even their brothers, what they had seen and heard on this mountain until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.
ch13.b027: The three were shocked. Risen from the dead? Only days ago they had reaffirmed their faith in him as the Deliverer and the Son of God, and they had just seen him transfigured in glory. And now he was speaking of death. Peter shuddered at the thought. It was more than he could bear to think about. Afraid that James or John might ask something about it, he hurried to change the subject and asked the first thing that came into his mind: why did the scribes say that Elijah must come first, before the Messiah?
ch13.b028: The Master knew that Peter was trying to steer away from any talk of his death. So he answered the question. Elijah did indeed come first to prepare the way, he said, and the Son of Man must suffer many things and in the end be rejected. But Elijah had already come, and men had not received him; they had done to him whatever they pleased. Then the three understood that he meant John the Baptist.
ch13.b029: At that name James’s steps grew heavy. John. The man who had cried repentance by the Jordan. The man beheaded in Herod’s prison. They had done to him whatever they pleased. Then the Son of Man too. James tried not to follow the thought any further. But he was not a man who could stop thinking. Ahead of him the Master’s back was dim in the starlight.
ch13.b030: As they went on down, the Master spoke again. They would not receive him as the Son of Man, he said, and so he had consented to be received according to their settled determination. But they should make no mistake: the Father’s will would prevail. If they chose to follow the inclination of their own wills, they must be ready for many disappointments and trials. Yet the training he had given them would be enough to carry them through even these sorrows of their own choosing.
ch13.b031: James buried everything he had heard that night in his heart. He would say nothing to his brothers. That would not be hard for him. He had always been a man who could keep silent for days. His brothers thought those silences a weakness, unaccountable spells. But this silence had a reason. And that reason he told no one until the day the Master rose again. Neither did Peter, nor John. They only turned it over in their own hearts.
ch13.b033: Before any of this happened on the mountain, around noon of that same day, something had happened at the camp below.
ch13.b034: From the start Andrew had not liked the conversation. The nine were sitting in a circle. Nobody could remember afterward who had begun it. But as always, the talk had drifted to the same place. Who would be greatest in the coming kingdom? Which places would go to whom? The Master had accepted their confession that he was the Deliverer and had at least admitted his divinity, and so they brought out again the hopes they had cherished so long. It was a day the Master was not with them, and those hopes were the first to lift their heads.
ch13.b035: Andrew wanted to stop it. But what could he say? If he told them to stop, they would think the chief was guarding the highest place for himself. He hesitated. It was a hesitation he would regret for a long time.
ch13.b036: Then people came crowding in. There was a man from Tiberias, James of Safed, with almost forty others who were looking for the Master. He was a minor official under Herod Antipas, and he had with him his only son, a lad of about fourteen. The boy suffered badly from epilepsy, and besides that he was possessed by one of the wandering, mischievous and rebellious midwayers who were then present on earth. For almost two weeks, the father said, he had wandered along the western borders of Philip’s domains looking for the Master.
ch13.b037: The nine apostles were greatly surprised and much disturbed. The mouths that a moment earlier had been arguing over places in the kingdom suddenly had nothing to say. Andrew stepped forward to greet the father and his son and asked whom they were seeking. The father said he was looking for their Master; he wanted him to cast out the devil that possessed his child. And he went on to tell them how the boy had suffered, and how many times the seizures had nearly cost him his life.
ch13.b038: Philip looked at the boy. A thin face, the marks of grinding teeth, bruises on his arms and legs. The child was clutching the hem of his father’s cloak. Without a word Philip fetched a skin of water and held it out to him. The boy would not take it. The father took it instead and wet the child’s lips. That was all Philip could do. He was a man of reckoning and provisions. Before a demon, his reckoning was no use at all.
ch13.b039: Then Simon Zelotes and Judas Iscariot stepped up to the father. They could heal the boy, they told him. There was no need to wait for the Master to come back. They were ambassadors of the kingdom, and they no longer kept these things secret. Jesus was the Deliverer, and the keys of the kingdom had been given to them.
ch13.b040: At that moment Andrew was off to one side, talking something over with Thomas. He turned his head at their words. Nathaniel and the others looked on in astonishment. All of them were aghast at the sudden boldness, if not the presumption, of the two. Into Andrew’s mind came Celsus’s garden. The keys. The Master had said they were authority over the outward affairs of the kingdom. He had not said they were authority over demons. But it was already too late.
ch13.b041: The father said that if they had been given power to do such works, he begged them to speak the words that would free his child from this bondage. Simon stepped forward. He put his hand on the boy’s head, looked straight into his eyes and commanded the unclean spirit, in the name of Jesus, to come out of him.
ch13.b042: The boy only had a worse fit. He fell to the ground and writhed. The scribes laughed. They were scribes from Jerusalem who had followed the Master’s trail all the way from Magadan. They pointed at the apostles and jeered. The believers who had come along had to bow their heads and bear the taunts.
ch13.b044: Andrew’s face burned. It was anger: at Simon and Judas, and before them at himself. He was the chief. He should have stopped this before it happened. No, before that, he should have put an end to that useless squabble over places. He called the apostles aside. Let us talk this over together, he said, and pray.
ch13.b045: The nine sat in a circle in the shade of a rock. No one spoke. Simon Zelotes stared at the ground. His hands were shaking. Judas was white in the face, but his mouth was shut tight. The twins leaned on each other’s shoulders. Matthew had his eyes closed and his lips were moving. Andrew tried to pray, but the scribes’ laughter was still in his ears.
ch13.b046: When the time of prayer was over, Andrew stood up. He felt more keenly than any of them the sting of their defeat and the humiliation that lay on them all. Somebody had to wash it away, and that was the chief’s task. He went to the boy. He tried once more to cast out the demon. He did not shout a command, as Simon had. He spoke quietly, earnestly. But the result was the same. The boy writhed again under his hands.
ch13.b047: Andrew drew his hands back. For a long moment he stood where he was. He could feel the scribes’ eyes fixed on his back. Then he turned. And he told the father plainly that they could not do it. He asked him to stay the night with them, or until the Master returned. Perhaps, he said, this kind would not come out except at the Master’s own command.
ch13.b048: It was the hardest thing Andrew had ever said. He had always been a man who got things done. If someone was hurt he bound the wound; if someone was lost he went and found him; if money ran short he found a way. Saying I cannot was not his way. Yet today he had said it, in front of everyone, in front of the jeering scribes. And strangely, once it was said, his shoulders felt a little lighter. Not pretending to have what he did not have: that much, at least, he could do.
ch13.b049: Philip came over to him. Without a word he pressed a piece of bread into Andrew’s hand. Only then did Andrew realize that he had eaten nothing all day.
ch13.b050: That night the nine could not sleep. They were confused and downcast, a dejected and chastened company. While the three were coming down the mountain in the starlight, full of what they had seen, the nine in the valley below knew nothing of it. James of Safed would not give up. Nobody could tell him when the Master would return, but he decided to stay. Philip made a place for the father and the boy to lie down and spread a cloak over them. Several times in the night the child had a fit. Each time, Philip got up and sat beside him.
ch13.b052: On Tuesday morning, a little before breakfast time, the Master and the three reached the camp. A crowd of about fifty had gathered around the apostles. They could hear loud argument from a long way off. The nine apostles, the scribes and the believers who had followed were split almost evenly.
ch13.b053: The nine were more than relieved to see the Master. And they saw the faces of Peter, James and John, which were strangely bright. That alone was enough to hearten the nine. They all ran out to greet the Master and their three brothers.
ch13.b054: While they were greeting one another the crowd came up, and the Master asked what they had been arguing about as he approached. The apostles could not answer. Before they could, the boy’s father came forward and knelt at the Master’s feet. His only son, he said, was possessed by an evil spirit. In his fits he cried out, foamed at the mouth and fell like a dead man, and sometimes the spirit threw him into water and even into fire. The boy’s life was worse than death, and his mother and he lived with broken hearts. Yesterday at noon he had found the disciples, and they had tried to cast out the demon but could not. Now would the Master heal his son?
ch13.b055: Andrew bowed his head as he listened. Could not. This time the words were spoken in front of the Master.
ch13.b056: The Master touched the father and told him to rise. Then he gave the apostles standing near him a searching look. Andrew did not avoid his eyes. To everyone standing before him the Master said: how long must he bear with this faithless and perverse generation? How long before they learned that the works of faith do not come at the bidding of doubting unbelief? And he told the father to bring his son.
ch13.b057: The father brought the boy. The Master asked how long he had been like this. Since he was a very small child, the father said. While they were talking the boy was seized again and fell down in their midst, grinding his teeth and foaming at the mouth. After a series of violent convulsions he lay before them like one dead. The father knelt again. If the Master could cure him, he begged, let him have pity on them and deliver them from this affliction.
ch13.b058: The Master looked down into that anxious face. He told the father not to question the power of the Father’s love, but only the sincerity and the reach of his own faith. All things were possible to the one who truly believed.
ch13.b059: Then James of Safed spoke, in words where faith and doubt were tangled together:
ch13.b061: Philip’s heart turned over when he heard it. Those were his words. They were what he had wanted to say all his life and never once had said. He had always asked to be shown. Show me and I will believe. But this man, without being shown anything, was saying that he believed and that he did not believe, both at once. He was bringing both and holding them out together. Philip learned that day, for the first time, that there could be such a prayer: faith offered without hiding the doubt.
ch13.b062: The Master stepped forward and took the boy by the hand. He would do this, he said, in keeping with the Father’s will and in honor of living faith. He told the boy to rise. He commanded the disobedient spirit to come out of him and never go back. And placing the boy’s hand in his father’s, he told him to go his way; the Father had granted the desire of his soul.
ch13.b063: The boy stood up. Everyone there, even the Master’s enemies, was astonished. It was a true healing of a double affliction, the sickness of the body and the sickness of the spirit together. From that hour the boy was well for good.
ch13.b064: Andrew watched the father take his son in his arms. For the first time the son was looking his father full in the face. Andrew looked away. Joy and shame came over him together. He had seen the thing he could not do done before his eyes. And he was glad of it. The gladness was larger than his humiliation. He thought that was a mercy.
ch13.b065: It was hard indeed for the three, who had so lately tasted the ecstasy of the mountain, to come down so quickly into the scene of their brothers’ defeat and confusion. But it was always so with these twelve ambassadors of the kingdom. They swung without rest between exaltation and humiliation. The Master told them they were going now to Caesarea-Philippi and should make ready at once. They walked south, a quiet group, with the crowd following behind.
ch13.b066: They spent that night at the house of Celsus. After they had eaten and rested in the garden, the twelve gathered around the Master. Thomas spoke up. Those of them who had stayed behind, he said, still did not know what had happened on the mountain, or what had made their brothers so glad. Since he understood that it could not be told now, would the Master talk with them instead about their defeat?
ch13.b067: The Master said that what had happened on the mountain would be made known to them in due season. And he would show them the cause of their defeat. While their brothers were on the mountain seeking the Father’s will, he said, they who stayed behind, though told to pray with him, had not used the faith they had. Instead they had yielded to temptation and gone back to their old habit of seeking preferred places in the material kingdom they persisted in imagining. No sooner did their faith take hold of who the Son of Man was, he told them, than the selfish wish for worldly advancement came creeping back.
ch13.b068: Andrew could not lift his head. The Master had not been there. And yet he knew what they had argued about.
ch13.b069: The Master went on. Such a kingdom did not exist, and never would. Had he not told them that whoever would be greatest must make himself small and become the servant of his brothers? In the thing they had tried and failed so completely to do, their purpose had not been pure: not their motive, not their ideal, not their ambition, not their method. And what they had tried to achieve was not the Father’s will. When would they learn that they could not do spiritual work without spiritual power, and could do nothing at all without the experience of living faith?
ch13.b070: Simon Zelotes sat at the end of the garden with his face in his hands. Judas sat just outside the circle of lamplight. His face could not be seen.
ch13.b071: As he finished, the Master said that he would now tell all of them what he had told their brothers on the mountain. The Son of Man was entering the last phase of his work. Before long, when he was delivered into the hands of those who sought his destruction, their faith and devotion would meet their great and final test. And they must remember: the Son of Man would be put to death, but he would rise again.
ch13.b072: They went to their beds in sorrow. They did not understand what he meant, and they were afraid to ask. Even the stolid twins were so shaken by it that they hardly slept that night. Not until after the resurrection did they remember all of it.
ch13.b074: Early on Wednesday morning they left Caesarea-Philippi. A little past the Waters of Merom, when they came to the Damascus road, the Master said they would go on to Capernaum by the road that crosses Galilee. The scribes and the crowd who would be following them would go down by the road east of the Jordan, reckoning that the Master and his apostles would be afraid to pass through the territory of Herod Antipas. The Master wanted to be alone with his apostles that day.
ch13.b075: Well past lunchtime they stopped in the shade to rest. After they had eaten, Andrew spoke to the Master. His brothers did not understand the Master’s deep sayings, he said. They had come to believe fully that he was the Son of God, and now they were hearing strange words about leaving them, about dying. Was he speaking in parables? He begged him to speak to them plainly, without veiling it.
ch13.b076: Even as he spoke, Andrew knew what he was asking. It was the very thing all of them had been afraid to ask the night before. Someone had to ask it. The chief asked it.
ch13.b077: The Master answered that it was because they had confessed him to be the Son of God that he must now begin to unfold to them how the work of the Son of Man on earth would end. They clung to the belief that he was the Messiah and would not let go of the idea that the Messiah must sit on a throne in Jerusalem. That was why he kept telling them that the Son of Man must soon go up to Jerusalem, where he would suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, the chief priests and the scribes, and that he would be killed and then raised from the dead. This was no parable, he said. He was telling them the truth, so that they would be ready when it came upon them.
ch13.b078: While he was still speaking, Peter rushed forward. He put his hand on the Master’s shoulder. Far be it from them ever to quarrel with the Master, he said, but he declared that such things would never happen to him.
ch13.b079: Andrew looked at his brother. The hand was gripping the Master’s shoulder hard. It was love. Andrew knew that. His brother had done it out of love. But the Master turned, to Peter and to the other apostles. His eyes flashed.
ch13.b080: The Master told them to get behind him. They savored of the spirit of the adversary, the tempter, he said. When they talked like that they were not on his side but on the side of the enemy. They were turning their love for him into a stumbling block in the way of his doing the Father’s will. They should set their minds not on the ways of men but on the will of God.
ch13.b081: It was as though the world had stopped. Peter’s hand fell from the Master’s shoulder. He stepped back. His face went white. Only a few times had the Master rebuked their shortcomings so sharply. He had always been patient with their weakness, but not when the path of carrying out the Father’s will to the end was threatened. The apostles stood there stunned, astonished and appalled, and none of them could find a word for the sorrow they felt.
ch13.b082: Andrew wanted to go to his brother. But his feet would not move. It was he who had raised the question. If he had not asked, his brother would not have reached out. And yet he also knew: someone had to ask. And the Master had to answer. His brother’s love was true, and the Master’s rebuke was true. He could only stand and watch the two collide.
ch13.b083: When the first shock had passed, and before they took to the road again, the Master spoke further. Whoever would follow him must disregard himself, take up his responsibilities day by day, and follow. Whoever tried to save his life selfishly would lose it, and whoever lost his life for the Master’s sake and the gospel’s would save it. What good would it do a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul? And they were not to be ashamed of him and his words in this sinful generation, even as he would not be ashamed of them before the Father.
ch13.b084: It was a painful road, full of conflict. To Galilean fishermen who still dreamed of a kingdom with places of honor for themselves, his words came as a great shock. Yet their loyal hearts were stirred by the courage of his call. Not one of them meant to leave him. He was not sending them into the fight alone. He was leading them.
ch13.b085: They walked on in silence toward Capernaum. As the afternoon wore on, the apostles talked a great deal among themselves, though not with the Master. Andrew went and walked beside the Master. No one heard what the two of them said. Peter walked at the very back. James kept close beside him. James could not speak of what they had seen on the mountain. But he knew what Peter had seen up there, and he knew how completely the man was broken now. Without a word, James matched his stride to Peter’s.
ch13.b087: At dusk they entered Capernaum. Keeping to the less traveled streets, they went straight to Peter’s house for supper. They stayed there while David Zebedee got ready to take them across the lake.
ch13.b088: Philip sat in the courtyard of Peter’s house. Peter’s children wandered in and out among the strange guests. Then the Master looked up at Peter and the other apostles and asked what it was they had been talking about so earnestly as they walked that afternoon.
ch13.b089: No one answered. Philip looked at the ground. Many of them had taken up again, on the road, the argument that had begun at Mount Hermon: who would be greatest. After such a rebuke the night before; after such a shock at noon.
ch13.b090: The Master knew what had been on their minds. He beckoned to one of Peter’s little ones and set the child down in their midst. The child looked up, not understanding, into the faces of twelve grown men. Unless they turned around and became more like this child, the Master said, they would make little progress in the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbled himself and became like this little one would be greatest in the kingdom. Whoever received such a child received him. And they must never despise one of these little ones, for their angels always looked upon the faces of the heavenly hosts.
ch13.b091: Philip looked at the child. The child was counting nothing: who was greatest, which place belonged to whom. He was simply sitting there, because the Master had called him. Philip thought of the twins, who on that January night before the ordination had fallen asleep by the garden fire before their turn came, and had been welcomed all the same. And he thought of the words he had heard the morning before in the valley from the boy’s father: I believe; help my unbelief. Philip went over what he had seen in a single day. He had not seen what happened on the mountain. But he had seen other things: a father on his knees, a boy standing up, Peter undone before a rebuke, and now this small child sitting among them. He thought it was enough. For a man who was always asking to be shown, it had been a day when a great deal was shown.
ch13.b092: When the Master had finished speaking, they got into the boat and crossed over to Magadan. The night sea was calm. Peter took the oars. Andrew sat facing him. Without a word, the two brothers rowed to the same stroke.
ch13.b094: The events follow Paper 158, “The Mount of Transfiguration”: the arrival at the foot of Hermon, the two days of preparation, and why only three were taken (158:0.1–0.3, 2.5); the ascent on August 15, the lunch halfway up, the Master’s absence from three to six o’clock and his words on returning, Peter’s question and the talk by the embers (158:1.1–1.7); the crackling sound, the vision of Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek, the three tents, the silvery cloud and the voice, and the hand that raised them (158:1.8–1.10); the charge of silence on the way down, the question about Elijah, the words on disappointments and trials, and the three men’s silence (158:2.1–2.4); the nine apostles’ dispute about rank, James of Safed, the attempt by Simon Zelotes and Judas, Andrew and Thomas in consultation, Andrew’s second attempt and his admission of defeat (158:4.1–4.8); the healing the next morning and the father’s words (158:5.1–5.5); Thomas’s question in Celsus’s garden, Jesus’ answer and the foretelling of his death and resurrection (158:6.1–6.6); the detour by the Damascus road, Andrew’s plea, Peter’s hand and the rebuke, the call to take up responsibilities daily, and the talk on the road (158:7.1–7.9); the child set among them at Peter’s house and the crossing to Magadan (158:8.1–8.2).
ch13.b095: Character facts come from Paper 139: Andrew’s appointment of the three as personal aides and his freedom from jealousy of his brother (139:1.3), James’s unaccountable silences and his ability to see all sides (139:3.3–3.4), James and John having known Jesus longest (139:3.1), and Philip’s wish “to be shown” and his work as steward (139:5.2–5.4).
ch13.b096: Fictional additions are small: the inner thoughts and memories of James, Andrew and Philip; the sensory details of the mountain, the starlight and the cloud; Philip handing over water and bread and watching over the boy at night; Andrew’s failure to stop the dispute about rank; how each man looked during the prayer; James walking beside Peter; and the closing scene of the brothers at the oars. The words of James of Safed are given as spoken dialogue, slightly reshaped. What Andrew and the Master said to each other on the road is not in the text, and so it is not invented here.
ch13.b097: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
